A crack just shot across this Roman wall and the rain is already running in.
Cracks like this can wreck concrete. But Roman concrete has a secret hiding inside.
It's full of little white lumps of lime. For years experts thought they came from sloppy mixing.
Then in twenty twenty three scientists at M.I.T. figured out what they really are.
The Romans mixed in quicklime, which gets so hot with water that it steams, and it leaves these lumps behind.
Now watch the crack. It runs right through a lump of lime.
Rainwater soaks into the lime and fills up with calcium.
That calcium hardens into new crystals that grow across the crack and seal it shut.
Scientists cracked test blocks made this way and ran water through them. Within two weeks the cracks healed and the water stopped.
Blocks made without quicklime never healed. The water just kept running through.
That's part of why the Pantheon is still standing almost two thousand years later.
Its dome is still the biggest ever built from concrete with no steel inside.
